vignette:
Layla, a 51-year-old social ministry worker, had spent decades building a life that kept her busy, useful, and most importantly, never still. She worked at a community outreach center in a bustling part of the city, coordinating food drives and visiting homebound elders. On paper, she was competent and dedicated. But her colleagues had noticed that Layla always chose a seat with a clear line of sight to the nearest exit, and that she would abruptly end one-on-one meetings to grab a coffee for herself and her visitor—an excuse to keep the office door open and to ensure she was never truly alone with another person.

The roots of this vigilance lay in a childhood she had never spoken about in full. Her father, a stern and devout man, had disciplined her with his hands and a leather belt, often in the small back room of their apartment. She remembered the way the room would darken as he closed the door, the smell of dust and his sweat. But when she tried to describe it now, words failed her. She could only feel the memory in her body: sometimes, without warning, her arms would curl protectively over her head, her knees would pull up to her chest, and she would find herself in a tight ball on the floor of her own kitchen, her heart pounding as if she were still a frightened child in that back room. The rage that followed was immediate and overwhelming—a hot, wordless fury that left her shaking and ashamed afterward. She couldn't explain to anyone why she sometimes screamed at her own empty apartment, or why she had to fight the urge to hit the wall.

Avoidance had become her lifeline. She avoided going to the center on days when she knew she would have to lead a small group alone; she called in sick or rearranged schedules. Over time, she began to dread even the thought of work. When she did go, her eyes darted to the corners of the room, and she frequently looked behind her as she walked from her car to the building, certain someone was following. She knew no one was there—logically, she knew—but the feeling was as real as the pain in her shoulders. Minor surprises, like a door slamming in the hallway, sent her into a full panic, her body bracing for a blow that never came.

Her irritability had grown worse over the years. She snapped at volunteers, she criticized the church secretary, she nearly drove away her closest friend. People began to walk carefully around her, which only confirmed her belief that she was dangerous, that she could not be trusted around others. She had come to believe that the only way to keep everyone safe—herself and others—was to never let anyone get close. Being alone with another person felt like an invisible cage closing in; the exit was not just a door but a symbol of her only chance at escape.

What finally brought Layla to seek help was not the anger or the checklists or the avoidance, but a single moment at the center. A young mother had come in with her toddler, and the child began to cry in a high, piercing way. Layla felt something snap inside her. She turned, walked out the back door, and sat on the curb, her body trembling, the rage so immense she could barely breathe. She could not for the life of her say what the memory was that had seized her—only that the sound of that cry had been a key to a lock she had tried to ignore for fifty years. She called a therapist the next day. She was terrified—terrified that if she opened that door, she would never be able to close it again, and terrified that the rage inside her would consume everything she had built. But she was equally afraid of continuing to live in a world where every closed door felt like a trap, and where the only safety she could imagine was to never stop running.
